item.title: Migrating the GitHub Copilot runtime to Rust, using Copilot
item.description: GitHub rewrote its Copilot agent runtime from TypeScript on Node.js into more than 800,000 lines of production Rust, a task primarily completed by a single developer over a few months with most code written by AI agents across 128 pull requests that shipped incrementally. The runtime, which backs the Copilot CLI, Copilot app, SDK, VS Code, Visual Studio, and other Microsoft and GitHub products, had originally been intertwined with the terminal UI and was later layered as an SDK on top of a headless CLI process, forcing out-of-process communication and roughly 100 MB of V8 overhead per client. Rust was chosen to enable in-process embedding via a C ABI, supporting six SDK language versions (C#, TypeScript, Python, Rust, Go, Java), while delivering lower startup time, memory use, and better scalability. Although the initial TypeScript estimate was 130,000 lines, approximately 430,000 lines of production TypeScript ultimately passed through the port alongside parallel incoming work. The migration improved runtime performance by orders of magnitude while the team continued expanding its capabilities.

item.title: Should you read the code, is RAG dead, and did Skills kill MCP?
item.description: A GitHub Podcast episode explores five AI hot takes by examining the assumptions behind them. Reviewing AI-generated code remains essential, but the level of attention should match the risk rather than treating every change the same way. Hiring managers increasingly value judgment about when and how to use AI over blanket adoption or refusal, with fluency in these tools becoming part of the craft. Skills and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solve different problems and work together, with MCP providing standardized interfaces and skills offering project-specific context and process guidance. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) remains valuable for grounding AI responses in relevant external information like documentation and internal knowledge. Finally, codebases that confuse AI models often confuse human teammates too, making maintainability, clear structure, and readable abstractions more important than ever.

item.title: Marketing ops as code: Automating events from planning to follow-up on GitHub
item.description: Tomoko Tanaka, who runs marketing for GitHub in Japan and Korea, automated her team's event workflows by converting written runbooks into GitHub Copilot conversations and GitHub Actions workflows. The system relies on three GitHub primitives: issue forms capture event details, labels trigger automations, and Actions execute the work. Planning begins with a conversation guided by an AGENTS.md runbook file, which helps draft campaign names and invitation emails before filing a structured GitHub Issue. Applying an "event-setup" label launches a workflow that duplicates event landing pages, generates UTM links, produces invitation emails, and files requests with relevant teams. A DRY_RUN repository variable allows the team to rehearse changes without affecting external systems, while daily cron jobs screen registrants and slash commands like /lead-upload and /event-report handle post-event tasks, all defined as SKILL.md procedures.

item.title: Coding Agents with an Obstacle-Aware Harness for Safe Robot Manipulation
item.description: The paper investigates whether coding agents—language models that write robot controllers as programs—can operate safely when tasks pair manipulation goals with obstacles that must not be touched. The authors find that such agents typically collide with obstacles because they treat task completion as their sole objective and never elevate the safety constraint to a true priority, even when they reason about the obstacle in their traces and the prompt forbids contact. By decomposing manipulation into a route phase and a contact-rich moment, they locate the failure in planning and contact execution. To address this, they introduce SafeHarness, which equips the model with two obstacle-aware harnesses: one for route planning using bounding boxes and waypoint-based candidate routes that are verified and replanned as needed, and another for contact execution that selects contact positions to avoid the obstacle. SafeHarness achieves 71.9% task success and 87.5% collision avoidance, surpassing prior state-of-the-art by 6.5% and 27.0% respectively.

item.title: Embedding Models Measure in Peculiar Ways
item.description: This paper investigates whether embedding models accurately reflect physical measurements of mass, distance, time, and volume, which have unique and objective notions of semantic equivalence and distance. The authors find that physical measurement is only weakly modeled in embedding spaces, with quite peculiar measurement patterns emerging instead. Further analysis reveals that embedding representations of physical measurements are strongly influenced by superficial string similarity rather than actual physical properties. Attempts at recalibrating similarity do not substantially improve the alignment between embeddings and true physical measurements. The findings suggest that embedding models fail to reliably encode objective physical relationships.

item.title: Workspace Models: Lightweight Robotic Memory via Saliency-Driven Supervision
item.description: Complex robotic manipulation tasks often require long-term memory of past events, but conditioning policies on full histories can introduce spurious correlations that hurt performance. While many existing methods rely on expensive vision-language model queries during deployment to filter for task-salient information, this paper proposes shifting those computationally intensive VLM calls to training time instead. The authors introduce the "workspace token," a lightweight latent memory representation trained in two stages: a VLM first identifies the current and historical information needed to complete a task, then this knowledge is distilled into the token via a set-reconstruction decoder loss. In both simulation and hardware experiments, the workspace token serves as a drop-in replacement for observations at deployment, enabling policies to solve memory-intensive tasks without in-the-loop VLM reasoning. Notably, the authors find that workspace tokens are not only more lightweight than full observation histories but also lead to better policy performance.

item.title: FAMOS: Feed-Forward 3D Articulation Modeling from Sparse Observations
item.description: FAMOS is a feed-forward model that predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from sparse, unordered sets of partial point clouds to model articulated objects. Unlike existing feed-forward methods that rely on a single observation and category-level shape priors, the model jointly reasons over multiple observations while naturally supporting a variable number of inputs, including single views. The authors introduce a Multi-state Articulation Transformer with alternating state-wise and global attention to aggregate articulation cues across observations. They also propose an observed articulation span objective that supervises the motion range each part exhibits across the input observations. To address limited dataset scale and diversity, they developed a procedural data generator that synthesizes self-annotated assets during training. Experiments on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K demonstrate consistent improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based baselines.

item.title: Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing
item.description: Paint-Anything, developed by Ji Xie, Dewei Zhou, Xinyu Huang, Zhennan Chen, and Xun Wang, enables any-color control in image generation and editing by letting users specify object target colors with 24-bit hex values. The method learns a shared hex-prompt interface for both tasks through object-level color supervision, avoiding dedicated color representations used in prior work. To train the system, the authors construct the Paint-500K dataset from real images via object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis. Because shadows make real-image labels only approximate, they add pure-color anchors whose pixels exactly match their paired hex values, applied only at high-noise timesteps. The paper also introduces ACBench, with ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit subsets, to measure object-level hex color fidelity. On FLUX.2-4B, Paint-Anything improves ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit scores by 85.3% and 28.3% respectively over the base model and achieves the highest average CompColor score among compared methods.

item.title: Jemalloc 5.4.0
item.description: Jemalloc 5.4.0 was released with over 160 commits focused on technical debt cleanup, including refactorings, bug fixes, test coverage improvements, option cleanups, and portability enhancements. New features include EXTENT_ALLOC_FLAG_PINNED for marking non-reclaimable mappings, new mallctl interfaces for reporting pinned-memory usage and mutex statistics, the ability to resume per-CPU arena selection via thread.arena, better alignment between human-readable and JSON malloc statistics, and the replacement of the runtime experimental_infallible_new option with the compile-time --enable-cxx-infallible-new option. Incompatible changes adapt tcache fill and retention targets per bin to demand between GC events and remove seven legacy non-experimental controls. Notable bug fixes preserve errno across free functions, fix numeric overflow checks in size classes, accept NULL in free_sized and free_aligned_sized, resolve TSD lifecycle edge cases, and address a potential arena_reset deadlock. The release also modularizes jemalloc's front end, simplifies ctl dispatch, introduces an OS abstraction layer, and provides portability improvements across macOS, MinGW, and GCC 16.

item.title: We made Playwright 2x faster and 80% more token efficient
item.description: Stagehand is an SDK designed for AI agents to extract data and interact with websites, available in TypeScript, Python, and Go. It builds on Playwright-style APIs like goto, click, locator, and screenshot while adding agent-focused capabilities: observe() returns real selectors so credentials never reach the model, act() self-heals when sites redesign, and extract() returns schema-validated data. Stagehand runs as a browser extension to reduce latency and offers features like WebMCP support, clipboard access, batch commands, and deep locators for nested iframes and closed Shadow DOMs. When pointed at the hosted Browserbase service, it executes 2x faster than Playwright cloud equivalents, with a Model Gateway that selects the cheapest model per action and server-side caching to avoid redundant token usage. The team also provides an MCP server for clients like Claude and Cursor, plus lightweight Search and Fetch endpoints for accessing web content without a full browser session.

item.title: Microsoft exec called AI scraping 'the largest theft of labor in human history'
item.description: Newly unredacted filings in The New York Times' copyright lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft reveal internal admissions that AI scraping amounts to theft and that AI products threaten publishers' livelihoods. Microsoft Applied Science director Brent Hecht called it "the largest theft of labor in human history" in a January 2023 memo, while OpenAI's Nick Turley described chatbots as an "existential threat" to publishers that are "largely substitutive." Microsoft data shows its Copilot answer engine reduced click-through rates to the NYT domain by as much as 93%, described internally as a "doom loop." Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that paywalled content should be licensed for training or grounding. The filings detail how the companies scraped content by bypassing paywalls, including an exchange where OpenAI's Greg Brockman replied "ah nice" to a paywall hack, and stripped copyright notices from training data before use.

item.title: I don't like passkeys
item.description: Computer science student Ethan Hawksley argues that while passkeys offer strong protection against phishing and data breaches, they are not yet mature enough for individual users due to risks of permanent lockout, automated account bans, and device loss. Hardware keys cannot back up passkeys, requiring users to purchase multiple keys per site, with limits of 25 to 300 accounts per device. Synced passkeys tied to Apple or Google accounts create a single point of failure, since an account ban could irreversibly lock users out of all third-party accounts. Third-party password managers like Bitwarden and KeePassXC still face fragmented platform support and inconsistent autofill experiences. For everyday users, the author recommends randomly generated passwords stored in a third-party password manager combined with an independent TOTP app, which he says provides better control and flexibility than current passkey implementations.
